charts.title: Segment EBIT-Adjusted Margin: GMNA vs GMI

ebitAdjusted.title: EBIT-adjusted
ebitAdjusted.content:
EBIT-adjusted is GM's own non-GAAP operating profit measure -- EBIT before restructuring, impairments and other items management calls one-off -- and is the number GM itself guides to each year.

For General Motors: it strips out the EV-realignment and China-restructuring charges that have repeatedly depressed GAAP net income, so it tracks the underlying automotive and financing business more smoothly than GAAP operating income does.

What to watch:

  • How often "adjusted" items recur -- repeated exclusions blur into ordinary cost of doing business
  • EBIT-adjusted margin trend, not just the dollar level, as GM's unit mix shifts

segmentMargin.title: Segment EBIT-adjusted margin: GMNA vs GMI
segmentMargin.content:
GM reports two vehicle segments plus GM Financial: GMNA (North America) and GMI (International, everywhere else). Each segment's EBIT-adjusted margin is segment EBIT-adjusted divided by segment revenue.

For General Motors: GMNA margin has historically run far above GMI's -- the North American full-size truck and SUV franchise is the profit engine, while GMI (including the retreat from Europe, Russia, India and most recently the China joint ventures) has been structurally thin or loss-making. The gap between the two lines is the story of where GM actually makes money.

What to watch:

  • GMNA margin compressing as incentives rise or EV mix dilutes truck/SUV profitability
  • GMI margin failing to recover despite restructuring, signalling further capital reallocation out of international markets

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue: GMNA vs GMI
segmentRevenue.content:
Segment revenue is third-party vehicle and parts revenue booked within each region before intersegment eliminations; it excludes GM Financial's revenue, which is largely interest and lease income rather than vehicle sales.

For General Motors: GMNA revenue is the dominant share of the consolidated top line; GMI's shrinking share reflects the exit from Europe, Russia, Australia/Thailand and the shrinking China JV footprint, so a falling GMI line is a strategic retreat, not just a weak quarter.

What to watch:

  • GMI revenue continuing to shrink as GM narrows its international footprint
  • GMNA revenue growth versus wholesale unit growth -- price/mix versus volume

wholesaleUnits.title: Wholesale units: GMNA vs GMI
wholesaleUnits.content:
Wholesale units are vehicles shipped by GM to dealers (in thousands), the volume GM itself controls and recognises revenue on -- distinct from retail/"delivery" units, which measure what dealers sell to end customers and can diverge from wholesales when dealer inventory builds or drains.

For General Motors: wholesale volume is the cleanest read on production and shipment trends by region, ahead of any price or mix effects baked into revenue.

What to watch:

  • Wholesale units running persistently above retail deliveries (channel stuffing / rising dealer inventory)
  • GMI wholesale volumes shrinking in step with the segment's revenue retreat

marketShare.title: Market share: US / China / worldwide
marketShare.content:
Market share is GM-badged retail/wholesale unit share of total industry vehicle sales in each market, as GM discloses it (annual only -- GM does not disclose share on an interim basis).

For General Motors: the US share has been comparatively stable (GM is typically the #1 or #2 seller), while the China share has collapsed over the past decade as domestic EV makers (BYD and peers) took volume from the SAIC-GM and SAIC-GM-Wuling joint ventures -- a major driver of the GMI segment's weak profitability and of GM's recent JV restructuring charges.

What to watch:

  • Further erosion in China share -- it is the single biggest swing factor in GMI's outlook
  • US share holding up against EV-focused new entrants

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For General Motors Company: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For General Motors Company: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For General Motors Company: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For General Motors Company: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For General Motors Company: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For General Motors Company: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For General Motors Company: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For General Motors Company: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For General Motors Company: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For General Motors Company: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue

dcf.base_sublabel: Owner FCF — after SBC, interest income & leases
dcf.model_approach_note: Implied P/E 51.5x (base IV 129.45 / FY2025 SBC-adjusted GAAP EPS 2.51) vs 10yr average 10.3x Step 8c.5 item 1, peak-earnings extrapolation: base rebuilt on mid-cycle owner FCF (inputs.mid_cycle_fcf 7,250 = mid-point of FY2021-25 median 6.9B and TTM 7.6B, SBC-adjusted); base EBITDA margin path 11.6-11.8% flat -> 11.2% gliding to 10.5% mid-cycle; bull plateau 13.0% -> 12.2% Step 8c.5 item 3, growth: base growth and terminal growth capped at the through-cycle automotive revenue CAGR of 1.5% (FY2010-FY2025, ex GM Financial); pre-fix 2.0-2.5% / 2.0% terminal; bull 3.5/3.0 -> 3.0/2.5 fading to 2.0 Step 8c.5 item 2, WACC: +1.0% extreme cyclicality and +1.0% regulatory/trade-policy premium on the 10% cost of equity = 12.0%, identical across scenarios; small-cap illiquidity not applicable; documented in inputs.wacc_rationale Step 8c.5 item 4, exit cap: no historical EV/EBITDA series exists (GMF lease depreciation pollutes consolidated EBITDA), so the P/E-based cyclical cap is used: terminal multiples 8/10/12x owner FCF = ~7/9/11x normalised earnings, under the 15-20x P/E ceiling; Gordon at 12% now sits below the base and bull caps weighted IV 121.58 -> 105.40 (mid-cycle flows and growth cap, -16.18) -> 93.89 (WACC +2%, -11.51); base 129.45 -> 94.29, bull 173.70 -> 132.51, bear 73.74 -> 67.47; see reconciliation.bridge P/E rule still trips at 37.5x because its denominator is FY2025 SBC-adjusted GAAP EPS of 2.51, a year carrying ~7B of EV-realignment and China charges (EPS-diluted-adjusted ~10.5); the market price of 86.16 is itself 34.3x that figure and no value above ~52 can clear the 20.7x line. On normalised mid-cycle earnings of 9.9-11.7/share the base IV is 8.1-9.5x, inside the 10.3x average. P/B and P/Sales pass. One fix pass only, per Step 8c; not iterated further.
